abstract: BACKGROUND: The literature on traffic-related air pollution and childhood cancers is inconclusive, and little is known on rarer cancer types. OBJECTIVES: We sought to examine associations between childhood cancers and traffic-related pollution exposure. METHODS: The present study included children < 6 years of age identified in the California Cancer Registry (born 1998-2007) who could be linked to a California birth certificate (n = 3,590). Controls were selected at random from California birthrolls (n = 80,224). CAlifornia LINE Source Dispersion Modeling, version 4 (CALINE4) was used to generate estimates of local traffic exposures for each trimester of pregnancy and in the first year of life at the address indicated on the birth certificate. We checked our findings by additionally examining associations with particulate matter (≤ 2.5 μm in aerodynamic diameter; PM2.5) pollution measured by community-based air pollution monitors, and with a simple measure of traffic density. RESULTS: With unconditional logistic regression, a per interquartile range increase in exposure to traffic-related pollution during the first trimester (0.0538 ppm carbon monoxide, estimated using CALINE4) was associated with acute lymphoblastic leukemia [ALL; first trimester odds ratio (OR) = 1.05; 95% CI: 1.01, 1.10]; germ cell tumors (OR = 1.16; 95% CI: 1.04, 1.29), particularly teratomas (OR = 1.26; 95% CI: 1.12, 1.41); and retinoblastoma (OR = 1.11; 95% CI: 1.01, 1.21), particularly bilateral retinoblastoma (OR = 1.16; 95% CI: 1.02, 1.33). Retinoblastoma was also associated with average PM2.5 concentrations during pregnancy, and ALL and teratomas were associated with traffic density near the child's residence at birth. CONCLUSIONS: We estimated weak associations between early exposure to traffic pollution and several childhood cancers. Because this is the first study to report on traffic pollution in relation to retinoblastoma or germ cell tumors, and both cancers are rare, these findings require replication in other studies.
abstract_ja: 背景：交通関連大気汚染と小児がんに関する文献は結論が出ておらず、希少ながんについてはほとんど分かっていない。目的：交通関連汚染への曝露と小児がんとの関連を検討する。方法：カリフォルニアがんレジストリに登録され、カリフォルニア出生証明書と連結可能な6歳未満の小児（1998〜2007年出生、n = 3,590）を対象とした。対照は、カリフォルニア出生名簿からランダムに選択された（n = 80,224）。妊娠各期および生後1年時点の出生証明書上の住所に基づき、CALINE4により交通曝露を推定した。PM2.5の地域モニタリングデータおよび交通密度の簡易指標でも検証した。結果：無条件ロジスティック回帰において、妊娠初期の交通関連汚染の四分位範囲あたりの増加（一酸化炭素0.0538 ppm、CALINE4による推定）は、急性リンパ芽球性白血病（ALL；妊娠初期OR 1.05、95%CI 1.01〜1.10）、胚細胞腫瘍（OR 1.16、95%CI 1.04〜1.29）、特に奇形腫（OR 1.26、95%CI 1.12〜1.41）、網膜芽腫（OR 1.11、95%CI 1.01〜1.21）、特に両側性網膜芽腫（OR 1.16、95%CI 1.02〜1.33）と関連していた。網膜芽腫は妊娠中の平均PM2.5濃度とも関連し、ALLと奇形腫は出生時の住所付近の交通密度とも関連していた。結論：早期の交通汚染曝露と複数の小児がんとの弱い関連を推定した。網膜芽腫または胚細胞腫瘍との関連を報告する初の研究であり、いずれも希少がんであるため、他の研究での再現が必要である。
